The role of operating systems in trusted AI
items.publisher: Brussels Privacy Hub, Vrije Universiteit Brussels
items.summary: Marco Bassini of Tilburg University moderates a CPDP 2026 panel on the role of operating systems in trusted AI, centred on interoperability under DMA Article 6(7). Alba Ribera Martínez argues that the Commission's specification decisions erode GDPR and security safeguards. Gary Davis of Apple lists what the Commission asks of Android, from hotword waking to live microphone, contacts, and screen access, and calls each a new attack surface. Karina Nimara of the Developers Alliance warns that bad actors will exploit unlimited access and that apps would compete for finite battery and processing power. Sebastião Barros Vale of the EDPS insists that the DMA leaves the GDPR intact, with OS providers and apps as separate controllers. Rob van Eijk explains the layered, sandboxed design of a phone OS and asks who consents when a user delegates decisions to an AI agent. Several panellists want the EDPS, ENISA, and independent experts to join DG Competition in this work.

items.publisher: Brussels Privacy Hub, Vrije Universiteit Brussels
items.summary: Cecilia Álvarez of Meta moderates a CPDP 2024 panel on the EU strategy for data, seen through AI and data protection. Rob van Eijk sets out how the data strategy, the DMA, the DSA, and the AI Act fit together, including Article 6(11) of the DMA and the AI Act timeline. Patricia Vidal, a competition lawyer, explains that dominance is not abusive in itself and that charging a fee is not abusive per se. Luca Bolognini calls for balancing rights with proportionality and practical rationality, and questions the EDPB's generic opinion on pay or consent. Peter Craddock argues that data protection reads necessity more strictly than contract law and that regulators overlook business realities. On pay or consent, Van Eijk applies proportionality and asks for alternatives for users who cannot pay.

items.summary: Rob van Eijk joins MEPs Brando Benifei and Francisca Hortal Foronda for a panel on digital regulation at the EU level, moderated by Kait Bolongaro. The panel follows the Belgian premiere of The Click Trap, a documentary about how digital advertising and micro-targeting fuel disinformation and threaten democracies.

Transatlantic Privacy Wire: Overheard in the EU
Prime[d] To Buy: Flash Sales And Deceptive Design
items.summary: The Advanced Study Institute of Asia (ASIA) launches its report Prime[d] To Buy on flash sales and deceptive design. Its researchers found deceptive patterns in all 26 Indian apps they studied, about five per app. They also found inflated discounts and Apple users paying more than Android users. Vasudevan then chairs a panel. Jhamb of Grant Thornton points to missing detection tools and audits. Rai of the Aapti Institute raises micro-targeting and the loss of trust, and Rajmohan of the Internet Freedom Foundation the weak enforceability of India's 2023 guidelines on dark patterns. Rob van Eijk explains how the EU's DMA and DSA address deceptive design, and how enforcement is changing cookie banners and consent flows on large platforms.

Privacy Through Innovation - Privacy Enhancing Technologies, Consumer Protection And The Online Ads Ecosystem
items.publisher: Brussels Privacy Hub, Vrije Universiteit Brussels
items.summary: Marek Jansen moderates a CPDP 2023 panel on whether privacy-enhancing technologies can reconcile online advertising with privacy. Anthony Chavez of Google presents the Privacy Sandbox, a set of purpose-built APIs that replace third-party cookies and combine on-device processing, secure enclaves, and differential privacy. Marie-Paule Benassi of the European Commission introduces the Cookie Pledge, which treats consent fatigue as a consumer protection issue. Stefan Hanloser of ProSiebenSat.1 argues that contextual advertising earns less than targeted advertising, and warns that the new APIs may favour large intermediaries. Rob van Eijk of FPF sees the APIs as a way to apply purpose limitation and data minimisation. He points to profitable contextual models and warns of AI-driven hyper-nudging. Christian Reimsbach-Kounatze of the OECD warns against PET hype and names cost, skills, and legal uncertainty as barriers.

Automated decision-making and profiling: lessons from court and DPA decisions
items.venue: ADM case law Report: roundtable discussion
items.summary: Rob van Eijk opens and Gabriela Zanfir-Fortuna moderates an FPF roundtable in Brussels on the FPF report on automated decision-making. Co-author Sebastião Barros Vale presents findings from more than 70 court and DPA decisions. The GDPR governs automated decisions well beyond Article 22, he finds. The Article 22 threshold itself is high, and enforcers interpret it differently, as in the Uber, Ola, and Clearview AI cases. Mireille Hildebrandt of VUB notes that trade secrets do not block an explanation of the parameters behind a score. Gianclaudio Malgieri of the Brussels Privacy Hub asks why gig workers see different outcomes and why data subjects carry the burden of proof. Brendan Van Alsenoy of the EDPS calls Article 22 a rule rather than a standard and sees a role for sector-specific rules, such as the platform work directive.

Does Consent work? If not Consent, what else?
items.summary: Vitor Jesus moderates a COnSeNT 2021 panel on whether consent works online and what could replace it. Armand Heslot of the CNIL states that a cookie banner with only an accept button does not give valid consent, because refusing must be as easy as accepting. Townsend Feehan of IAB Europe presents the Transparency and Consent Framework as a tool to comply with GDPR and ePrivacy. Robin Berjon of The New York Times calls the TCF a configuration string. He argues for needing less consent, for example by ruling out third-party controllers. Irene Kamara of Tilburg University calls letting users choose legitimate interest unlawful, and points to the Radio Equipment Directive to make standards binding. Mark Lizar argues for consent receipts that people keep themselves. Rob van Eijk explores privacy preferences set in browsers and devices.

items.title: Technology for Privacy: Protecting Against Online Tracking and Profiling
items.publisher: Brussels Privacy Hub, Vrije Universiteit Brussels
items.summary: ENISA organises this CPDP 2018 panel, chaired by Athena Bourka and moderated by Kai Rannenberg of Goethe University Frankfurt. It asks how technology can protect users against tracking and profiling across devices and apps, in line with the GDPR and the proposed ePrivacy Regulation. The speakers are Rob van Eijk of Leiden University, Mike O'Neill of BayCloud, Diego Naranjo of EDRi, and Fenneke Buskermolen of the European Commission. The panel covers the main techniques for online and mobile tracking, how privacy by design can help, and best practices for preventing tracking and obtaining consent.

items.title: Do Not Track, is self-regulation enough?
items.summary: MEP Amelia Andersdotter chairs a European Parliament event on whether self-regulation is enough for Do Not Track. Robert Madelin of DG CONNECT calls tracking creepy and a risk to the information base of democracy, and argues that self-regulation can work if it is accountable. Rob van Eijk of the Dutch DPA, who represented the Article 29 Working Party in the W3C, states that in the EU Do Not Track means do not collect without consent. He urges industry to innovate with user-centric design. Nicolas Dubois of DG Justice, standing in for Paul Nemitz, explains how the data protection reform handles tracking through the right to object and codes of conduct. Stuart Hamilton of IFLA raises e-readers that monitor reading habits. Justin Brookman of CDT and Walter van Holst of EDRi question whether the narrow W3C standard can deliver what EU law requires.

items.title: IPEN Workshop 2014
items.summary: Achim Klabunde of the EDPS moderates the first panel of the IPEN Workshop 2014, on the gaps between existing privacy tools and what people need. Florian Stahl and Stefan Burgmair present the OWASP Top 10 Privacy Risks for web applications. Hannes Tschofenig of ARM explains how the IETF and the W3C build privacy considerations into standards. Jens Kubieziel traces how Tor evolved, including its defences against censorship. Joss Wright of the Oxford Internet Institute notes that privacy keeps moving up the development stack and that academic cryptography rarely reaches products. Stéphane Petitcolas of the CNIL shows what mobile apps leak in practice. Rob van Eijk of the Dutch DPA frames privacy as a fundamental right shaped by purpose and context. Most data flows, he notes, happen beyond the device and out of view.

items.title: Who is following me: tracking the trackers
items.summary: Christine Runnegar of ISOC and Sophie Kwasny of the Council of Europe co-moderate an IGF 2012 workshop on tracking the trackers. Rob van Eijk, a PhD student at Leiden University who represents the Article 29 Working Party in the W3C Do Not Track debate, explains that unique identifiers, from cookies to browser fingerprints, are the core of tracking. The European position, he says, is "do not collect" without consent. Wendy Seltzer of the W3C describes the Do Not Track standard in progress. Cornelia Kutterer of Microsoft explains why Internet Explorer 10 sends Do Not Track by default. Kimon Zorbas of IAB Europe calls that default paternalistic and argues that limits on behavioural advertising favour large platforms. Malavika Jayaram of CIS India describes Indian rules that make cyber cafés identify and log their users.

items.title: Strictly Speaking: Cookies, Consent and Compliance
Legal perspectives on anonymization
items.venue: Future of Privacy Forum De-identification Workshop Day
items.summary: David Hoffman of Intel moderates the closing panel of a Future of Privacy Forum workshop on what re-identification research means for the law. Daniel Solove of George Washington University Law School presents PII 2.0, which treats identifiability as a continuum of risk and applies fewer Fair Information Practices as the risk falls. Jane Yakowitz of Brooklyn Law School argues that the value of public research data outweighs realistic re-identification risks. She proposes a safe harbour for data producers who apply basic anonymisation, and penalties for recipients who re-identify. Harley Geiger of CDT turns to health data and cautions that a ban on re-identification would hamper security research. Rob van Eijk of the Dutch DPA, speaking for himself, treats re-identification as further processing that needs a legal ground. He proposes managing privacy risk like security risk. The discussion turns to First Amendment limits on penalising re-identification.
